To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a long-term rise in Mediterranean saltwater export, induced by a cooling of the Indian Ocean and the subsequent reduction of African monsoonal rains, triggered an increased flow and cooling of Mediterranean Outflow Waters (MOW), that in turn, led to a long-term rise of Upper North Atlantic deep-water formation and a phase-lagged cooling of the Labrador Sea.

1) The Plio-Pleistocene Mediterranean Outflow Water (MOW) was a major source of heat and salinity for the Atlantic Ocean and 2) The MOW flow was affected by a combination of changes in the Indonesian Through-Flow (ITF) and the Atlantic Meridional overturning Circulation (AMOC).

1) the Mediterranean Sea was the major driver of the Atlantic meridional circulation in the Late Pliocene, 2) the Atlantic meridonal circulation was driven by changes in the Indonesian Through-Flow, 3) the Mediterranean Sea and the Indonesian Through-Flows were connected via the Indian Ocean, and 4) the Indonesian Through- Flow was driven by a change in the Earth’s orbit.

the following aspects: (1) the ultimate, geodynamic control of changes in circulation of Mediterranean outflow water on Atlantic meridonal overturning circulation, (2) the potential impact of changes on the distal advection of Mediterranean outflow on the climate of the NE Atlantic, and (3) the role of the Mediterranean Sea in Pliocene climate change.

a long-term increase of salt discharge from the Mediterranean Sea into the North Atlantic after ~3.5 Ma, induced a unique long-lasting rise in the formation rate of Upper North Atlantic deep water, which was a key driver of the Pliocene global climate system.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the Indonesian Through-Flow was a major player in the Pliocene climate system and that the MOW was a major player for the Atlantic meridional thermohaline circulation.
the Pliocene Mediterranean salt export, and thus the Atlantic overturning circulation, were controlled by changes in the Indonesian Through-Flow, rather than vice versa.
a long-term cooling of the Indian Ocean was ultimately responsible for an increased MOW discharge and a rise in Atlantic meridional circulation activity.
